form: As a corollary to Wayne Suttles’ conclusions in ‘Some Questions about Northern Straits’, I am presenting a Native perspective on the relevance of family connections and oral tradition to Nothern Straits dialects.

form: The family trees of Charley Edwards, Lena Daniels and Tommy Bob were compiled by me from my personal field notes (1968-present). Throughout the years my consultants have been my late mother Eva Guerin, Al Charles, Theresa Gibbs, Lena Daniels, Ivan Morris and Emma Edwards. In addition, I have consulted secondary sources such as the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) records, tribal enrollment records, school records, census records, archival records and church records.

form: My sources for the above genealogies are documents from the BIA, a notarized deposition by David Tom dated July 7, 1917, genealogies compiled by Wayne Suttles, and my own field work with Emma Edwards. In Figure 1, I tried to regularize the orthography of the names that I took from Wayne Suttles’ field notes1 because the genealogy program I use has no phonetic type. However, I have kept intact the names I took from the BIA records.
I have used a capital “E” for schwa and “lh” for the voiceless lateral fricative. In addition, I have used “ch” for the post alveolar affricate.

form: On July 7, 1917, a notary public for the State of Washington residing in La Conner, deposed David Tom who stated that he was born about 1850 at the Lummi Reservation. He said he was Lummi, and so was his father. His mother’s father was also Lummi, but his mother’s mother “was a La Qualan—a small band near Lummi.” (Notarized document July 7, 1917).

Charley Edward identified the language spoken by the Samish, Lummi, Saanich and Songhees as Ləkʷəŋínəŋ. Tommy Bob who identified himself as Samish also used this term to refer to his language. (See Suttles this volume.) When Lena Daniels visited Lummi in 1996, I asked her directly what she called herself. Without hesitating, she answered, “Lummi”.

gloss: Northern Straits, the Samish, as Tommy Bob named himself

form: From my Native point of view, it seems to me that at one time these families all spoke the same language Ləkʷəŋínəŋ. I ask myself, do they now speak different languages, or do they still speak one form or another of Ləkʷəŋínəŋ.
